newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco pact proponent sees congressional talks.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco pact proponent sees congressional talks.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent
Talks in Congress about a possible settlement to the skyrocketing number of lawsuits against cigarette makers could start early next year, a key proponent of an accord said.

"I expect some movement on this in the next congressional session. I can't tell you exactly what form it will take but I expect some movement and I expect to be involved," said Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore, who has been pushing for a settlement.

Moore, who spoke in a telephone interview on Thursday night, cautioned that a final settlement could take some time, if one is reached at all, and was unlikely before three state lawsuits against the industry go to trial next year.

He said talks among some state attorneys general and plaintiffs lawyers aimed at a settlement have been escalating. But he said the group has not yet met directly with tobacco officials and continues to work through intermediaries.
"We've been meeting about it a lot. I'm real optimistic," he said.
Moore pointed to recent remarks by RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. Chief Executive Officer Steven Goldstone as possible evidence that top ranking executives would consider an accord.

In a Dec. 5 speech to executives in Boston, Goldstone said that many forces were at work favouring a settlement with the tobacco industry. "In 1997, the most meaningful thing I can do is come to some solution on this problem."

Daniel Donahue, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. senior vice president and deputy general counsel managing the tobacco litigation, denied that his company was in any settlement talks and said it planned to fight the suits.

"We are not in the process of any kind of negotiations or discussions of any kind of settlement primarily because these attempts by plaintiffs lawyers to twist and turn the litigation system of this country are basically wrong," he said, adding he expects to "successfully defend" the cases.

Growing speculation about a possible legislative solution comes as the tobacco industry faces massive legal fights on numerous fronts. Eighteen state attorneys general, New York City, and the California cities of San Francisco and San Jose and counties including Los Angeles have sued the industry to recoup health care costs of smokers.
Moore predicted eight more states will also file lawsuits in coming months. The new Congress convenes on Jan. 7.
In addition, at least 13 class-action lawsuits have been filed in state courts by smokers and others. In Florida alone one plaintiffs' lawyer has filed about 300 individual cases.
Suits by Mississippi, Florida and Texas seeking to recoup the costs of health care for poor smokers are scheduled for trial next year along with at least two of the class actions.
The industry is also under fire from federal investigators and regulators.
The Justice Department is conducting several criminal probes of the industry on allegations that it hid crucial information from federal agencies and investors.
The Food and Drug Administration has proposed regulating the advertising and marketing of cigarettes. The industry is challenging the restrictions with arguments set for February.

Legal and investment experts said it will be nearly impossible to reach an accord that would satisfy all of the attorneys general, plaintiffs lawyers and the industry. Such a settlement would most likely have to involve a legislative solution that would indemnify tobacco companies against lawsuits while providing big payoffs to injured parties.
Despite incredibly difficult and lengthy negotiations, many believe a legislative solution will eventually be the only way to put an end to litigation.

Mary Aronson, a Washington, D.C.-based institutional investment advisor, said that a $750,000 verdict by a Florida jury in August against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp. was a sign that the attitude of the public was changing.

"That kind of vulnerability may be good for the industry. It will force them to consider some sort of deal," Aronson said, predicting that a settlement would boost the prices of tobacco company stocks.
She said the industry should reach a deal before some of the bigger cases go to trial, while its hand is stronger than it would be after a loss.
"I think they would be foolish to wait until then (losing a case)," Aronson said. "If the plaintiffs bar starts winning cases, they will be much harder to buy off."
Brown & Williamson is owned by Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc.
